questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Please explain: *
Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had visited UNIMI before and the university and city seemed to fit what I wanted to experience during my Erasmus. I knew they had a great faculty of philosophy, something I wanted to explore - an opportunity to have courses that interested me, and wasn't necessarily related to my studies in Rhetoric at Copenhagen Uni. Another aspect was my familiarity with italian culture - I have traveled there a lot, but I wanted to experience how an everyday life would look like. To have a structured stay while experiencing another culture was crucial.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy: the staff at UNIMI was ready to help with necessary questions. But I would say that to have a backbone, some kind of fundament, which I had with fellow students from UCPH, helped a lot. If the staff at Unimi couldn't help, we just tried out different stuff, which eventually helped. To be transparent with the knowledge you gain along the way. Otherwise I would say that Unimi was helpful with their mails. They sent a lot of helpful mails along the way, while reassuring that everything would be okay - that we just needed to be patient. They were professional while laid back - it was great.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The students helped each other a lot. To have a network between students was quite helpful. The staff at UNIMI was also helpful - sending us mails. Also we asked the professors if we had any questions regarding the semester, the structure etc. But to find out answers yourself in a new city was also character-building one might say.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was okay - everything is kind of a leap of faith trying to find housing in another city. But Spotahome was great - a lot of the students from Cph used spotahome, and as far as I know almost everyone had a good experience. For me personally it was easy - of course you get nervous, but when everything was set, it felt quite smooth.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: That it is a leap of faith, but just trust the process. Everything will work out. And of course that you get to experience a local neighbourhood. That you'll find your own little café, a little cinema, that you'll become familiar with the city, and get a great relationship to this city - you'll hopefully get some friendly relations with the locals, getting to know their first name etc.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration is done at their site Unimia. Unimi sent a mail that described how you register for both exams and courses - so this part went quite smooth. Where it gets messy is when trying to find out which courses you want, and to plan them so they don't overlap. This part can take some time, because not all classes and their time-schedule are released at the same time. Therefore you must be patioent and trust the process. It will take time; it can get chaotic and messy, changing courses throughout the stay. My recommendation therefore is to try to keep updated, and just attend a class that you found interesting, just one time to see if it's something for you. You can always restructure your courses, something Unimi was quite open about.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Talking to other students, speak to the professors. This way you get a sense of what the courses are about, how they are structured, how they teach etc.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Quite successful, everything worked out eventually. I wanted to focus on philosophy and intellectual history - and that's what I got.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Show up to different classes, speak to the professors and the other students. But also, don't think too much of it, sometimes it's okay to stick with your initial feeling, and not change courses too much: this way you don't fall behind, and also; which clarity comes freedom, freedom to explore the city, and a not so worried mind regarding the courses. It brings calmness to do it quick, and then stick with it. Sometimes the course you thought was interesting actually isn't all that, but then just stick with it - too much changing around can create chaos, so rather spend your energy drinking Apperol Spritz and eat great food than worrying about courses - trust your gut.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of the courses very generally speaking lower than at UCPH. The amount of reading was generally lower than at Cph, and the 'background' knowledge of humanities (theories, history etc.) was lower - sometimes I got quite surprised by the difference in basic-common-ground knowledge. And also the level of participation; at cph I'm used to a high level of debating and participation in class, but at unimi it wasn't the culture, it was more listening to the professor without questioning anything - the critical awareness was lower. But this is okay: then you'll experience both academia and the culture.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching was generally constituted by lectures with presentations. The professor spoke, the class listened. In Cph you're invited to debate and discuss the text - this was not the case at Unimi. Some professors tried a bit, but the culture among the students was generally just listening without questioning.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.answer:

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Language and Metaphysics. The students were fun, and philosophy is a huge faculty in Milan. You'll get to make some presentations regarding the topic, and to debate and share examples is a huge part of this course. Which always a great thing. And the atmosphere is great among the students; you can disagree on certain things, but nothing gets personal, which is very important! So if you want to get stimulated by debating the students and the professor - this class is for you.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: There were some costs regarding the housing - some Italian tax. But generally nothing was unexpected: I knew that a lot of my budget would go to eating out, going out in the evening etc.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: everything was generally speaking cheaper than in Copenhagen: but the supermarkets was extremely cheap compared to Cph: you could live really well for a small amount of money.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: quite many; didn't attend anything

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to the Cinema! The culture of cinema is huge in italy and milan. Small cinemas, big cinemas, outdoor cinemas. You'll get to meet the locals, have a chat over a beer. And it's really cheap! 6 euros for a ticket. At the Cinema was were i hanged out; and where I met a lot of locals.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the Cinema! Or take a train to Genova or Como, swim a little. The train system in italy is really good, and cheap. So take a look where you want to go, and just book a ticket; it can be great to 'reset' the city you live in, and return with an open set of eyes again.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy: the locals were all very friendly! But the italians like to run late. So just chill out, thats what the italians like to do.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just speak to them

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not much actually - thats just personal I think; I loved every bit of the culture, and it wasn't challenging to adjust.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness of italians. Very friendly everyone. Thats something I'll take with me; to have an open mindset, to just relax and chill out; grab a drink if necessary. Of course the weather helps with this, but I'll try to incorporate this lifestyle in Cph. We could all learn a little by this.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Trust the process.
Everything will eventually work out.
Don't stress.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To have a personal connection to another city. To learn about the italian culture, and to incorporate this in your own life. It's not necessarily something you'll notice right away, but when you return you can definitely feel the difference. And also a lot of great and unique stories!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Honestly, I dont know: for me, everything was just as I dreamed of. Sometimes I missed talking my own language, but alora; then you'll recognize how crazy and lovely it is that you're actually living in another country. It's a great opportunity.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
